en: The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra, one fascicle;
the Dharma for Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts as Inquired by Upāli,
translated by the Śramaṇa Guṇavarman of Kapiśā during the Song dynasty.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes the precepts, accomplishes the virtuous precepts, and accomplishes the precepts for benefiting sentient beings, they should first fully train in and perfect the upāsaka precepts, the śrāmaṇera precepts, and the bhikṣu precepts.
If one says that it is possible to obtain the śrāmaṇera precepts without being fully endowed with the upāsaka precepts, such a thing is impossible.
Likewise, it is also impossible to obtain the bhikṣu precepts without being fully endowed with the śrāmaṇera precepts.
It is likewise impossible for one who does not possess these three kinds of precepts to obtain the bodhisattva precepts.
For example, it is as with a four-storied tower: it is impossible to reach the second story without passing through the first;
it is also impossible to reach the third story without passing through the second, or to reach the fourth story without passing through the third.

Once a bodhisattva has fulfilled these three kinds of precepts and wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should, with a sincere mind and free from greedy attachment, relinquish all internal and external things;
if one cannot relinquish them, the three precepts will not be complete, and one will ultimately be unable to obtain the bodhisattva precepts.

At that time, the recipient, observing his own body as one would observe a wise person, should then, in a quiet place, pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions. Facing east before an image, with his right knee touching the ground and palms joined, he should say:
"May the Virtuous Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Sangha of the ten directions listen!
Now I, [Name], seek the Bodhisattva precepts.
I have already fulfilled the Upāsaka precepts up to the duties of the wise; therefore, I seek the Bodhisattva precepts from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saṅghas of the ten directions.

Now, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saṅghas of the ten directions observe my mind; if I possess a lack of faith, a mind that disparages the bodhicitta, an evil mind, or a deceitful mind, do not bestow the precepts upon me;
if I am free of these, you should bestow the precepts upon me out of compassion.
The second and third times were also thus.
Having remained silent with a sincere heart, focused in mindfulness, he spoke these words:
"Now you have bestowed the Bodhisattva precepts upon me."
I have already obtained the Bodhisattva precepts. Why is this?

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions observe my mind with their knowledge of others' minds; since I possess a sincere mind, you should know that they have already bestowed the precepts upon me out of compassion.
"Now I have no teacher; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions are my teachers.
He says this a second and a third time.
At that moment, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions manifest signs; one should know that the precepts have been obtained.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions addressed the great assembly:
"In that world, such-and-such a person has truly received the bodhisattva precepts; we have now bestowed them out of compassion."
"Now this person has no teacher; I shall act as his teacher. I now protect and mind him; he is my dharma-brother.
Having said this, he immediately rises and pays homage to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; this constitutes the self-ordination (*svakarmavācanā*).
If there is a wise person who, out of pride, does not receive [the precepts] from them, one does not obtain the Bodhisattva precepts.

However, if the person is a breaker of the precepts; or if the wise person is in a distant land; or if the country is in turmoil; or if one is personally ill; or for the sake of benefiting many people; or if there is no other place to receive them—then whether one is a monastic or a layperson, if they can relinquish [worldly concerns] and practice giving, establishing a vow with a profound mind to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, if there is one who shares the same bodhicitta, the same Dharma, and the same intention, who is able to explain and instruct, and who well understands the meaning, the person wishing to receive the precepts should go to that person’s place, prostrate with their head at their feet, baring the right shoulder, placing the right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, say:
“Virtuous One, listen attentively!
I now beg the Virtuous One to grant me the Bodhisattva precepts, the precepts of great sovereignty, the unsurpassed precepts, and the precepts of invincibility.
If the Virtuous One does not hold me in high regard, out of compassion for me, I beg you to bestow these precepts upon me.

If that Venerable One remains silent and listens, you should immediately rise again, adjust your robes, and prostrate with your head at the feet of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the Great Grounds. According to the power of your own wisdom, praise all the merits of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, maintain single-minded mindfulness of the Triple Gem, and, kneeling for a long time with palms joined before the Buddha image, speak these words:
"Venerable One!..."
I, [Name], now request to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Venerable Sir,
out of compassion, please bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon me now.

If that Venerable One remains silent and listens, the recipient at that time should single-mindedly and with a focused mind take refuge in the Triple Gem, give rise to a heart of joy, and further reflect:
"Now I have attained the accomplishment of an immeasurable, boundless, and unsurpassed treasury of merit; I shall now receive the precepts upheld by Bodhisattvas."
Furthermore, one should remain silent with a single-minded focus.
At that time, the wise person says to the recipient:
"Good son, listen attentively!"
Dharma-brother Bodhisattva!
Are you now truly a bodhisattva?
Have you truly given rise to the bodhicitta?
The recipient replied:
"Venerable sir,
it is indeed so."
The wise one spoke again:
"Do you now fully possess the three kinds of precepts? He replied:
"Endowed. He asked again:
"Are you able to relinquish all things, both internal and external?"
He replied, "I can relinquish it.
He was asked again:
"Do you cherish your body and wealth? He replied, "I do not."
He asked again:

"Are you able to receive from me all the bodhisattva precepts, the precepts that encompass the entire path to enlightenment, and the precepts for benefiting all sentient beings? Are you able to uphold these precepts, which are identical to the precepts of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the three periods of time?"
He replied, “I can.
A second and third time, he did likewise.
At that time, the wise person should utter these words:
"May the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of Great Virtuous Sangha listen!
Now, so-and-so requests me; he seeks to receive the Bodhisattva precepts from the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Sangha of the ten directions."

Having already fulfilled the three precepts and generated the bodhicitta, you are a true Bodhisattva, capable of relinquishing all internal and external possessions and not sparing even your own body or life.
Out of compassion, may the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Saṃghas of the ten directions bestow the Bodhisattva precepts upon [Name].

Out of compassion, they bestow the precepts of the immeasurable, boundless, and unsurpassed treasure-trove of merit, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings and for the increase of the Dharma of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The second and third times were also like this.

At that time, a cool breeze arose from all directions. The wise should know that the Buddhas and the assemblies of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, having bestowed the precepts upon this person, say to the recipient:
"Listen attentively, [Name]!
The Buddhas and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas of the ten directions now bestow upon you the precepts.
Just as the bodhisattva precepts of all those of the three periods of time are maintained, you should uphold them with a sincere heart.
Are you able to uphold them?
He replied, “I can.
A second and third time, he did likewise.
At that time, the wise one pays homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Sangha of Bodhisattvas, and the images of the Buddhas; having paid homage, he further proclaims these words:
"May the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great virtue in the ten directions listen!"
Now that this person [Name] has made the triple recitation, they have received the bodhisattva precepts from all the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
I am the one who proclaims them; [Name] is the one who receives them; and I serve as the witness for [Name].
The "Great Master" refers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Sangha of the ten directions, who are immeasurable in number; the "Little Master" refers to myself.
There are two kinds of masters: first, those who are visible; [and second, those who are invisible].
Second, the invisible.
The invisible refers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Sangha of the ten directions;
the visible refers to my own body.
"From a teacher, whether visible or invisible, this person has completed receiving the precepts.
A second and third time it was likewise said.
Thus the *karmavācanā* was concluded.
When the *karmavācanā* was concluded, both remained silent.
At that time, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, having perceived this sign, addressed the great assembly:
"In that world there is such a person as this, who has received the Bodhisattva precepts from that wise one."
"Such a person as this is my Dharma-son; I now regard them with sincere compassion and protective mindfulness.
Because the Buddhas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas regard them with compassion and protective mindfulness, both the giver and the receiver shall increase in wholesome dharmas.
Having remained silent for a short while, he then rose and paid homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Sangha of Bodhisattvas.
This is called a Bodhisattva having received the Bodhisattva precepts.

These are the universal precepts, the unsurpassed precepts, the boundless precepts, the precepts that are a mass of merit, the precepts of tranquility, the precepts of a pure mind, and the precepts that shatter the afflictions of all sentient beings. Such precepts as these surpass all the precepts of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas throughout the ten directions.
Why is this? It is for the sake of liberating all sentient beings.
Once a bodhisattva has received the bodhisattva precepts, they should study and recite the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-vinaya.

When a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they should first conduct an examination: if the candidate lacks faith, they should not receive them from such a person. Likewise, those who are stingy, greedy, or insatiable; those who break the precepts, defile the precepts, or do not respect the precepts; those who delight in greed and anger; those who lack patience; those who cannot restrain others from transgressions; those who are indolent, lazy, or who crave worldly pleasures and take delight in mundane affairs; even those who cannot bring the Three Jewels to mind for a single moment; those caught in the net of doubt and the darkness of ignorance; and those who cannot recite the Bodhisattva Dharma-piṭaka or the Bodhisattva Vinaya, or who even go so far as to slander them—such persons one should not receive the precepts from.
Once the precepts have been received, one should not speak of them to those who lack faith, nor even to those who revile the Mahāyāna.
Why is this? Because those who do not believe will, by reason of this, fall into hell; therefore, a bodhisattva should not speak of them to such people, for if they do speak, they incur an offense.
A Bodhisattva knows with certainty that if one speaks to such a person in order to destroy their evil verbal karma and their lack of faith, there is no fault in speaking.
Once a Bodhisattva has received the Bodhisattva precepts, the teacher should explain to them the dharmas regarding what constitutes an offense and what does not.

If he knows that the student is able to receive [the precepts] with a sincere heart—receiving them not for the sake of making offerings, not to emulate others, and not out of pride—then at that time the teacher should explain to him the rules concerning what constitutes an offense and what does not:
"Listen attentively, [Name]!
The Bodhisattva precepts consist of eight grave rules (*gurudharma*).
Four of these are as previously described.

If a bodhisattva, for the sake of seeking gain and offerings, praises himself by claiming to have attained the bodhisattva precepts and to dwell on the bodhisattva stages, this is called the fifth grave rule for a bodhisattva.

"If there are those who are poor and suffering from affliction, as well as the sick, who come to beg for alms, and yet the bodhisattva, out of greed and stinginess, does not give even a single coin; or if there are those who seek the Dharma, and he, being parsimonious, does not give even a single verse—this is called the sixth grave offense of a bodhisattva."

"If a bodhisattva becomes angry, they should not inflict harm; yet if they strike with their hand, or with a staff or a stone, or revile them with harsh words; or if at times, being powerless, they cannot strike or revile but harbor anger and resentment in their hearts; or if they are struck or reviled by another and, when that person seeks reconciliation, they do not accept the apology, thereby harboring resentment that increases without ceasing such that the mind is impure—this is called the seventh grave offense of a bodhisattva."

"If a bodhisattva has a fellow teacher or fellow student who slanders the Vaipulya Dharma-treasury of the bodhisattvas, or who receives, studies, and upholds teachings that are merely similar to the Dharma but are actually non-Dharma, one should not dwell with them;
if one knows this for certain, one must not praise their virtues before others. This is called the eighth grave dharma of a bodhisattva."
“There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:
first, those who live at home;
second, those who have left the home life.”
There are six grave offenses for those living at home and eight grave offenses for those who have gone forth.

If a bodhisattva commits these eight grave dharmas—if he commits each grave dharma in its entirety—he will be unable to adorn immeasurable, unsurpassed bodhi in the present, nor will he be able to bring his mind to tranquility in the present; such a person is called a bodhisattva in name only, not a bodhisattva in reality.
Such a person is called a *caṇḍāla* among bodhisattvas; they are not called a śramaṇa, nor are they a brāhmaṇa, and they are unable to proceed directly toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The bodhisattva mind has three grades: inferior, middling, and superior. If one commits an offense with the inferior or middling mind regarding the latter four grave transgressions, it is not termed an "offense";
however, if one commits them with a superior or an evil mind, it is termed an "offense."

The "superior" refers to one who delights in performing these four kinds of actions, whose mind lacks shame and remorse, who does not know how to repent, who fails to recognize their transgressions, and who praises those who break the precepts; this is called the superior offense of an evil mind.
Although a bodhisattva may commit these four grave offenses, they ultimately do not lose the bodhisattva precepts.

For example, if a bhikṣu commits the four grave offenses, he loses the prātimokṣa precepts; likewise, if a bodhisattva commits the four grave offenses of a bhikṣu, they also lose the prātimokṣa precepts and defile the bodhisattva precepts.
"Defiled" means that in the present one cannot adorn bodhi, nor can one attain immeasurable merit or samādhi; this is called being defiled.
There are two causes and conditions by which one loses the bodhisattva precepts:
first, the regression of the bodhicitta.
Second, one may encounter a mind of extreme malice.
Free from these two conditions, even if one falls into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts in future lives, one shall never lose the bodhisattva precepts.

The Bodhisattva precepts are not the same as the Prātimokṣa precepts; if a bodhisattva receives the Bodhisattva precepts again in a future life, it is not called "newly obtaining" them, but is termed "revealing and polishing them to purity."

Now I shall further explain the characteristics of what constitutes an offense and what does not, as well as the distinctions of lightness and gravity, and the differences between the superior, middling, and inferior grades, regarding the reception of the bodhisattva precepts.

"If a bodhisattva, having already received the bodhisattva precepts, fails for even a single thought-moment during the day or night to offer flowers and incense, to prostrate before, or to praise with a joyful heart the stupas, images, sutras, or those who read and recite them—whether they be thousands or tens of thousands of bodhisattvas—this is called a grave offense, yet it is not termed one of the eight grave offenses."
This is called a bodhisattva having a defiled mind or a doubting mind; it is like having a wound that falls away and gives rise to impure thoughts.
If one acts without a heart of reverence, due to lack of faith and due to indolence, this is called a grave offense, but it is not called one of the eight cardinal transgressions.
If one lacks a mindful mind, this is called a minor offense.
There is no offense if one possesses a pure mind and constantly seeks bodhi.
A pure mind is like the fourfold faith possessed by a srotāpanna.
"If a bodhisattva is not content and does not have few desires, becoming greedily attached to gain and offerings, this is called a grave offense, but it is not called one of the eight grave offenses.
There is no offense if he can certainly know that through being discontented he is able to discipline sentient beings."

"If a bodhisattva, upon seeing a senior elder, one of long-standing virtue, a fellow student, or a fellow teacher, gives rise to a mind of arrogance or ill will, fails to rise to greet them, pay homage, or offer them a seat; fails to engage them in conversation or inquire after their well-being with a friendly disposition; or, when questioned about a doubt, fails to provide an explanation—this is called a grave offense, yet it is not called one of the eight cardinal transgressions."
This is called the bodhisattva’s defiled mind and doubting mind; it is like having a wound that falls away and fails to arise as purity.
There are instances where an action is performed without transgression: when one is ill, asleep, or when the mind is distracted.

When listening to the Dharma with a sincere mind as an offering to the Buddha—whether transcribing, reading, reciting, explaining, or discussing its meaning—one should speak with guests and others while protecting the speaker’s mind. One should know that by refraining from speaking, one can bring about discipline, for the sake of preventing violations of the monastic rules and out of consideration for the many.

“If a bhikṣu, seeking out faults, listens to the Bodhisattva precepts but does not believe or accept them, or does not believe in the teaching; or one who has not accomplished the upāsaka precepts, has not accomplished the śrāmaṇera precepts, or has not accomplished the prātimokṣa precepts—such a person may not listen to the Bodhisattva precepts. To listen [under such conditions] constitutes an offense.”
If a bhikṣu who has committed a pāyattika offense listens to the bodhisattva precepts without shame or remorse, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣu who has committed a sthūlātyaya offense listens to the bodhisattva precepts without shame or remorse, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu who has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, being without shame and without remorse, listens to the bodhisattva precepts, he incurs a pārājika offense.
Regarding the eighth grave offense, if one speaks of it [to such a person], one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who lacks faith should not listen; one who lacks faith should not speak.

If a donor of profound faith invites a Bodhisattva—whether to his own home, a stūpa or monastery, a village, or a kingdom—and provides all necessities such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine—if the Bodhisattva, out of arrogance, malice, or contempt, does not go to accept these offerings, he commits an offense. This offense is committed due to afflictions.
"If a bodhisattva goes alone without a companion to the home of a layperson, they incur a fault of error.

If, having arrived at the house of a layperson, they are unable to preach the Dharma, provide instruction, and transform them so that they may make offerings to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, this is called a grave offense, but it is not called one of the eight grave offenses."

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one is dull-witted; if one is insane; if there is a distant invitation; if there are dangers or difficulties on the road; if one knows that by not accepting the invitation it will lead to the taming of the other person; if one has already accepted a previous invitation; if one is diligently practicing wholesome dharmas; if one has not yet heard the meaning and wishes to hear it; if one knows the host’s intention is not sincere; if one fears that many people would become resentful were the invitation accepted; or if it is prohibited by the Sangha.

"If there is a donor who offers a bodhisattva gold, silver, pearls, musaragalva, agate, lapis lazuli, crystal, male and female slaves, vehicles, elephants, horses, and other such items, as well as various colored rugs and furnishings, the bodhisattva should accept them; if he does not accept them, he incurs an offense. This offense is committed due to afflictions."

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is insane; if one knows that upon receiving it, greed and attachment will certainly arise; if one knows that after receiving it, the donor will feel regret; if one knows that after the donor has given, they will go insane; if one knows that after receiving it, the donor will become impoverished; if one knows that these items belong to the Three Jewels; if one knows that these items were obtained through robbery;
if one knows that upon receiving them, one will experience much suffering—namely, royal persecution, bandits, death, imprisonment, the spread of a bad reputation, or being banished from the country;
or if one knows that upon receiving them, one will be unable to relinquish or utilize them to cultivate merit in a virtuous field of merit.

"If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of understanding the meaning, desire to hear the Dharma and dwell in the presence of a bodhisattva to inquire about what they have not yet heard, and the bodhisattva, with a frivolous mind or a conceited mind, does not explain it to them, he incurs an offense. This offense is committed due to afflictions."

There is no offense if one knows that the person before one holds evil and heterodox views and seeks out faults; or if one is ill; or if one has recently recovered from illness; or if one is insane; or if one knows that by not speaking, that person will be disciplined; or if the Buddha has not yet established a precept; or if one knows that the person does not give rise to reverence toward the Triple Gem; or if their conduct is coarse and negligent; or if one knows that upon hearing profound meanings, a person of dull faculties will give rise to heterodox views; or if one tolerates heterodox views; or if one knows that after hearing it, they will turn to evil people and proclaim the matter, thereby destroying the True Dharma.

"If there are wicked people who commit acts of killing or are outcasts (caṇḍāla), and if a bodhisattva does not associate with them, visit them, or preach the True Dharma to them, he incurs an offense."

Why is this? If a bodhisattva sees one who upholds the precepts and is diligent, with body, speech, and mind purified, yet fails to give rise to compassion toward them; whereas seeing an evil person, they are able to give rise to compassion—for this reason, if the bodhisattva does not speak for such a person's sake, they commit an offense.

There is no offense if one is insane; or if it is due to royal decree; or if it is due to a monastic regulation; or if one considers that many people would be displeased; or if one knows that by not speaking, the person will be brought to discipline.
"If there is a donor who is not a relative—whether a householder or a brahmin—who offers various kinds of robes to a bodhisattva, the bodhisattva should accept them."
If a bodhisattva seeks for himself a large quantity, he may accept it.
As it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls.
As it is with robes and alms bowls, so it is with thread.
If a bodhisattva goes to a donor to request thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it, instructing them to weave it tightly and ensuring it is broad and thick;
saying, "I shall not wear it myself, but you and the donor will both have merit."
If a donor says, "I do this for the sake of my teacher; I only wish that you would wear it yourself," and the Bodhisattva,

having received it, goes to a weaver for his own sake and instructs him to weave it tightly and make it broad and thick, then if he receives the robe and wears it himself, he commits a grave offense, though it is not termed one of the eight heavy offenses.
If one does not teach [the precepts], there is no offense.
"Once a bodhisattva has received the bodhisattva precepts, they should accept and possess silk bedding, even up to hundreds of thousands of millions in number; the same applies to gold and silver."
Śrāvakas act solely for their own benefit; therefore, the Tathāgata does not permit them to accept or possess [these things].
Bodhisattvas are not like this; because they act for the benefit of sentient beings, he permits them to possess them, and they must not fail to accept them.

If one refuses [to accept offerings] for the sake of contentment or reputation, one incurs an offense of loss of intention (*āpatti-āśaya*), falls into a state of non-arising, and whatever one does will be accompanied by doubt and impurity.
If a bodhisattva, due to the cause of indolence, is unable to benefit sentient beings, they incur an offense; this offense is committed through the afflictions (*kleśa*).

"If a bodhisattva is praised by others as being one of the ten stages, yet remains silent and accepts such praise when they are actually an arhat down to a srotāpanna who possesses few desires and is content with little, they commit an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions."
If a bodhisattva enters the midst of the Saṃgha and sees people engaging in unrighteous joking and laughter, it is an offense if he does not rebuke them.

It is not an offense if, while listening to the Dharma, he does so for the sake of disciplining them, for the sake of teaching the Dharma according to their inclinations, or for the sake of being able to benefit them.
"If one says:
'The bodhisattva neither delights in nirvana nor does he not delight in it; he neither fears afflictions nor does he not fear them. Why is this?'"
"Because they circulate through birth and death.
If a bodhisattva speaks these words, they commit an offense. Why is this?
The bodhisattva’s delight in nirvāṇa is such that it cannot be known by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

The nirvāṇa in which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas take delight does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or even an infinitesimal fraction of the bodhisattva’s delight.
The bodhisattva’s revulsion toward and fear of afflictions is something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot comprehend.

Compared to the bodhisattva’s revulsion toward and fear of afflictions, the revulsion toward and fear of afflictions held by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas does not equal even one part in a hundred, one part in a thousand, or one part in a hundred thousand million, nor even a single infinitesimal fraction thereof.
Why is this? Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas seek only their own benefit and are unable to benefit others;
Bodhisattvas are not like this, for they benefit both themselves and others.

Although a bodhisattva practices amidst outflows (āsrava), they are superior to an arhat; for while dwelling amidst outflows all day long, they are not defiled by afflictions (kleśa). Therefore, [the arhat] incurs an offense.
"If a bodhisattva does not fear ill repute and does not guard against ill repute, they incur an offense of loss of mind."
If one speaks ill of another when that person has committed no evil or transgression, one incurs an evil offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions.
If one employs harsh words for the purpose of subduing [the other], one incurs an offense of regretful mind (āpatti-vinidhāya), but it is not an evil offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one rebukes those who are non-Buddhists pretending to have come to receive the Bodhisattva precepts; if the mind was originally without malice but harsh words were uttered involuntarily; if one is insane or deranged; if one knows that the reprimand will bring great benefit; if one knows that by being angry with them, they themselves will obtain benefit; if one incurs an offense because one failed to give rise to anger for the sake of protecting the precepts; or if one knows that by being angry with them, they will obtain a small benefit in the present life but no great benefit in future lives.

If a bodhisattva strikes back at one who strikes them, reviles back at one who reviles them, or harasses back at one who harasses them, they incur an offense of negligence; this offense is committed due to afflictions.

"If there are bodhisattvas who mutually criticize one another—whether their criticisms be true or false—the bodhisattva should immediately humble themselves and offer an apology; if they are unable to do so, they incur an offense.
If they do not accept the apology offered, they likewise incur an offense."
Because of negligence, one incurs an offense if one does not accept an apology.
Because of negligence, one incurs an offense if one does not grant an apology.

There is no offense if one knows that the person has been habitually wicked and constantly seeks out others' faults; or if one knows that by not accepting the apology, one will cause that person to abandon their evil ways.
"If a bodhisattva harbors resentment toward another and constantly thinks,
'When I see him, I shall beat or scold him,' and fails to cease or desist from this, being unable to discipline himself, he commits an offense."
"If a bodhisattva travels along the same road as a bhikṣuṇī, there is no offense.
If he has a mind of lust, he incurs a transgression.
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of taming [the bhikṣuṇī]."
"If a bodhisattva receives food from a nun who is not a relative, there is no offense.
Why is this? Once a bodhisattva-mahāsattva has generated the bodhicitta, among all sentient beings there are none who are not their relatives."
If a bodhisattva, driven by greed, keeps many disciples, he commits an offense.
There is no offense if it is for the sake of taming them, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, for the sake of benefiting others, or if he is free from a greedy mind.
"If a bodhisattva is indolent and lazy, not diligent and energetic, and delights in sleep and reclining, he incurs an offense.

There is no offense if he is ill; or if his strength is insufficient after recovering from illness; or when traveling a long distance; or when exhausted from reading and reciting; or when contemplating the remedies."
"If a bodhisattva engages in idle talk concerning worldly affairs, they commit an offense.

There is no offense if one speaks because another has asked, or if one speaks according to another's disposition for the sake of their discipline, provided that one speaks with a sincere mind and does not add to or subtract from the truth."
"If a bodhisattva, out of a mind of arrogance, does not consult a teacher or receive the teacher's instructions, they incur an offense.

There is no offense if one is ill, insane, deluded, or exceptionally brilliant, learned, and wise; or if it is for the sake of disciplining sentient beings; or when one has entered meditative concentration."
"If a bodhisattva, when a desire-thought arises, does not examine the antidote and swiftly pacify it through skillful means, they commit an offense.
There is no offense if, although they have examined the antidote, the power of the afflictions is so intense that they cannot cause it to be extinguished;
or if they intentionally test themselves by deliberately giving rise to a desire-thought."
"If a bodhisattva says:
'One should not receive the precepts of the śrāvakas, nor should one read the sūtras of the śrāvakas. Why is this?'"
"Because the Śrāvaka sūtras and vinayas cannot benefit all sentient beings.
If one speaks thus, it constitutes a grave offense, yet it is not called one of the eight grave offenses.
There is no offense for one who acts out of attachment to the sūtras and vinayas of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
"If a bodhisattva does not read or recite the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, but instead exclusively reads and recites the sūtras and vinaya of the śrāvakas, they commit an offense.
There is no offense if they have not heard of or known the existence of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
If a bodhisattva does not read or recite the true scriptures of the Tathāgata, but instead reads or recites worldly treatises, verses, or commentaries, they commit an offense.
There is no offense if it is for the purpose of engaging in debate to refute false views, or if two parts are devoted to the Buddha’s scriptures and one part to external texts.

Why is this? It is because one knows that the external scriptures are false and deceptive teachings while the Buddha-dharma is true; it is because one understands worldly affairs and is not held in contempt by worldly people.

"If a bodhisattva, upon hearing of inconceivable matters within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka or the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, does not believe or accept them, but declares them to be 'not the word of the Buddha'—whether this is their own slander or the slander of another—they incur an offense."
If a bodhisattva should say:

"My power of wisdom is weak and my fleshly eye is impure; I do not see the profound realm of the Tathāgata. The realm of the Tathāgata is seen by the Buddha-eye and is known only by a Buddha; the entire dharma-realm is beyond my reach."
If one can contemplate and observe in this manner, it is called "practice through realization.
Whether the bodhisattva practices patience or not, neither constitutes a transgression.

However, if a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of anger or pride and says of himself, "My observance of the precepts, learning, and wisdom are all superior to yours," he incurs an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions.

There is no offense if it is for the purpose of destroying wrong views, for the purpose of overcoming those who hold the Buddha’s Dharma in contempt, for the purpose of subduing their arrogant minds, for the purpose of engendering faith in those who have not yet believed, or for the purpose of increasing the faith of those who already possess it.
If a bodhisattva hears that there is a place where the Dharma is being taught and does not go to listen even as far as one yojana away, they incur an offense.
If they do not go because they disparage the speaker, they incur an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions.
If one fails to go due to indolence, one incurs an offense of negligence.
There is no offense if one does not perceive, does not know, or has not heard [of the event]; or if one is ill; or if one has recently recovered from illness and lacks sufficient strength;
or if one knows that the speaker will present the Dharma erroneously and improperly; or if one fears that the speaker might give rise to feelings of shame or embarrassment.

Whether it be a teaching of a single dharma that has no further meaning, or the cultivation of wholesome dharmas, or the transformation of sentient beings, or if one does not understand that teaching, or is unable to recollect it.

"If a bodhisattva treats those who preach the Dharma with contempt, failing to give rise to reverence or praise their virtue, and mocks what they say because the words and meanings are not correct, they incur an offense."
"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, does not participate in the affairs undertaken by sentient beings, they commit an offense.

That is to say, if they do not join them in coming and going, entering and exiting; in guarding and protecting property; in reconciling disputes; in performing various virtuous deeds; or in observing the precepts, practicing generosity, and cultivating extensive learning, they commit an offense."

There is no offense in the following cases: if one is ill; if one does not know how to perform the action; if one is engaged in a major personal undertaking; if one has previously promised to assist another; if one is cultivating wholesome dharmas for oneself; if one fears that many people would become angry; if one is joyful, deluded, or insane; if one knows that the person cannot be disciplined by such means; or if it is prohibited by the Sangha.

"If a bodhisattva treats one who expounds the Dharma with contempt, reviles, strikes, or mocks them, and relies solely on the literal words of what is said rather than its meaning, they commit an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions."

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, is unable to act in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, they commit an offense—namely, in their walking, standing, sitting, and lying down while practicing various wholesome deeds."
If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, sees a person suffering from illness and is unable to provide care or act as an attendant for them, they commit an offense.
There is no offense if the bodhisattva themselves is ill.
If one lacks the power of resources, one should extensively exhort and convert those who do possess such power.

Or, if that patient has many kinsmen; or if one is urgently practicing the unsurpassed wholesome Dharma oneself; or if one has previously attended to the illnesses of others; or if one's faculties are dull and obtuse.
As it is with illness, so it is with poverty and suffering.

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, sees sentient beings who are evil and practicing unwholesome dharmas, yet fails to instruct, rebuke, or exhort them, they commit an offense of negligence."

There is no offense if one knows that this person has a virtuous friend who can instruct and reprove them; or if one knows that although they have been instructed, they do not follow those words; or if one has reached a state of understanding the language; or if the other person harbors harmful intent.
"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, possesses items identical to those of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), they commit an offense of negligence (*manasikāra-āpatti*).

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, should not receive food or drink using vessels made of gold or silver; the copper vessels they possess must not be the same as those of a layperson, and the use of wooden or horn vessels is strictly prohibited. To use them constitutes an offense."
There is no offense if the original vessel is lost, if one is on a journey when invited, or if one is gravely ill.
If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, fails to acknowledge the kindness [of the donor], they commit an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions (*kleśa*).
"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, receives a favor from another and is unable to repay it, they commit an offense.
One who repays it should maintain the precepts, practice with diligence, engage in seated meditation, and recite the scriptures; they should repay the favor by doing whatever the donor delights in."
There is no offense if the donor does not accept [the gift].

"If a Bodhisattva, having received the Bodhisattva precepts, sees a person in distress—whether suffering from death, loss of property, kings, thieves, water, or fire, or separation from relatives—he should go to that person's location to preach the Dharma and offer consolation, providing whatever they require according to his own capacity."
If one is unable [to comply], one commits an offense.

There is no offense if one does not have autonomy, if one is seriously ill, if one has not received the instruction, if there are difficulties or obstacles, if the king is hostile toward that person, or if the Sangha has established a prohibition.

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, takes on disciples but is unable to seek from faithful donors the necessary clothing, food, bedding, medicine, and dwellings for them to be provided at all times, and furthermore fails to teach and transform them through preaching the Dharma at appropriate times, he commits an offense."

There is no offense if one knows that the disciple possesses great power, intelligence, and merit, and has many donors; or if one knows they are a follower of a non-Buddhist path who has come deceitfully to steal the Dharma; or if one knows they will not be able to cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish.

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, should constantly praise the good deeds of others, yet conceals the virtues of another, they commit an offense; this offense is committed due to afflictions."

There is no offense if the person prevents it; or if they are distracted, dull-witted, or unaware; or if one is seriously ill; or if one considers that others might be offended; or if the matter is difficult to discern, such as the case of the *āmra* fruit and so forth.
"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, sits upon a bed or couch that exceeds eight finger-widths in height, he incurs an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when preaching the Dharma, when accepting an invitation from a donor of sincere faith, or when sitting within the temple of a non-Buddhist."

"If a bodhisattva, having already received the bodhisattva precepts, fails to become angry when one ought to be angry among his disciples, fails to reprimand when one ought to reprimand, fails to punish when one ought to punish, or fails to expel when one ought to expel, he incurs an offense; this offense is committed due to affliction."
If one becomes angry when one should not be angry, rebukes when one should not rebuke, punishes when one should not punish, or expels when one should not expel, one incurs an offense.

There is no offense if one knows that the disciple is capable of burning a stupa or monastery and committing great evil deeds; or if they might kill their own preceptor (*upādhyāya*), or a fellow preceptor or fellow *upādhyāya*, or their parents; or if one is waiting for the right time; or if one knows with certainty that due to such causes and conditions the monk will bring about schism in the Saṃgha; or if one knows that at a later time the person will spontaneously feel shame and remorse.

"If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, acquires great supernormal powers and yet does not feel fear when encountering those who should inspire fear, or does not inspire faith in those who should be inspired with faith, he incurs an offense."
There is no offense if one knows that all [beings] believe in heterodox and inverted views and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma.

If a bodhisattva, having received the bodhisattva precepts, constantly maintains a sincere mind and does not harbor thoughts of transgression, yet should happen to commit one, they must immediately confess and repent before others—specifically those of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna who are well-versed in the meaning of the teachings and capable of explaining them eloquently.
This is called the "all-encompassing precepts" of a bodhisattva.

From the bodhisattva’s first stage (*bhūmi*)—wherein one understands the six *pāramitās*—up to all-encompassing precepts, everything therein constitutes the bodhisattva’s prohibitive precepts; this is termed "all-encompassing precepts."
That which the Tathāgata did not previously teach in the sūtras for the śrāvakas, he now teaches in the Vinaya of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
For what reason is it called "all-encompassing morality" (sarva-śīla)?
Because it summarizes the precepts for both the ordained and the laity, this constitutes all precepts.
Regarding "difficult precepts," there are three kinds:
first, when a bodhisattva possesses great sovereignty and immeasurable wealth yet is able to renounce them all to receive the bodhisattva precepts—this is called a difficult precept.

Second, when a bodhisattva faces urgent distress or peril, they do not allow even a slight flaw or fracture in their precepts, much less their total destruction; this is called the difficult-to-observe precept.

Third, although a bodhisattva follows sentient beings in walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, they always firmly uphold the precepts without allowing them to be violated; this is called the difficult-to-observe precept.
"There are four kinds of all self-restraint:
first, that which is undertaken;
second, that which is innate."
Third is cultivation;
fourth is skillful means.
"Receiving" refers to the three *karmavācanās*.
"Nature" refers to that which is coexistent with nature; this is because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s nature is supple.

Regarding those who constantly cultivate wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, and who have practiced skillful means under immeasurable Buddhas and various Bodhisattvas—just as these Bodhisattvas gather in sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and instruct them to cultivate and accumulate goodness of body, speech, and mind—this is called "all self-restraint."
"The precepts of a virtuous person are of five kinds:
first, personally upholding the prohibitive precepts;
second, teaching others to uphold them;"
Third, praising the precepts;
fourth, seeing those who joyfully uphold them and rejoicing in their praise;
fifth, repenting for any transgressions immediately so that the mind never ceases its effort—this is called the precept of virtuous persons.
“There are thirteen kinds of those who practice the precepts of all formations:
first, making vows and dedicating merit toward nirvāṇa;
second, being vast;”
Third is purity; fourth is joy;
fifth is non-breach.
Sixth, non-dragging;
seventh, firmness;
eighth, the necklace.
Ninth is reality;
tenth is meaning;
eleventh is faith.
Twelfth is the jewel;
thirteenth is the constant.
Just as with the prohibitive precepts of the śrāvakas in the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, all wholesome dharmas are causes for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is called the morality of all practices.
“There are eight kinds of violations of the precepts; a bodhisattva should always maintain this reflection:
‘Just as I do not delight in death, so it is for all sentient beings. Therefore, one should not kill living beings.’”

Just as I do not delight in robbery, greed, sexual misconduct, harsh speech, lying, double-tongued speech, idle chatter, or striking and reviling others with sticks or stones, so it is with all sentient beings. Therefore, one should not engage in robbery, greed, sexual misconduct, harsh speech, double-tongued speech, idle chatter, or striking and reviling others with sticks or stones; this is called the precept of removal.
Even at the cost of losing their body and life, Bodhisattvas shall never violate these eight precepts.

Regarding the precept of benefiting oneself and others, a Bodhisattva must refrain where there is a prohibition and act where there is permission; if one does not refrain where there is a prohibition or does not act where there is permission, one incurs an offense.

The Bodhisattva knows which sentient beings may be gathered and gathers them, and which may be relinquished and relinquishes them; with pure precepts of body and speech, they constantly practice together with the *dāna-pāramitā*, up to practicing together with the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Such pure precepts benefit both oneself and others, and are thus called the "precept of benefiting self and others."

"Regarding the precept of tranquility: from the initial reception of the precepts until their firm maintenance with the mind, one does so for the sake of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and for the fruit of a bodhisattva, not for the sake of body or life; this is called the precept of tranquility."
When a bodhisattva is seated, if they see a king or an elder and rise, they commit an offense.
If they have already assumed the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), and upon seeing a king or an elder they kneel, they commit an offense.
If one’s robes were previously disarrayed, yet one restrains one’s demeanor and adjusts one’s clothing upon seeing a king or an elder, one incurs an offense.
If a king or an elder utters harsh words, yet one praises them according to their whim, one incurs an offense.
To give rise to doubt where there is no cause for doubt is an offense. To fail to give rise to doubt where there ought to be doubt is an offense.

Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts: during the first and last watches of the night, one must not sleep; one must be fully endowed with virtuous vows, virtuous conduct, and wholesome dharmas; one must be capable of employing right livelihood; one must remain far removed from the views of annihilationism and eternalism while practicing the Middle Way; one must be free from the pleasures of the five desires, being unsurpassed and peerless; and one must remain far removed from false views, neither breaking nor destroying them—this is called the precept of tranquility.

The Bodhisattva’s assembly of precepts is accomplished, fully endowed with immeasurable and wondrous fruits; by virtue of these causal conditions of the assembly of precepts, one fulfills the śīla-pāramitā.
Although the recipient has not yet attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they have already attained the fullness of five kinds of meritorious qualities:
first, they are constantly kept in mind by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Second, they experience eternal, pure bliss;
third, they have no regrets at the time of death;
fourth, upon casting off the body, they attain rebirth in the worlds of all Buddhas.
Fifth, it adorns *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One who upholds the bodhisattva precepts does not act for their own sake, but solely for the benefit of others and to adorn *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This bodhisattva precept is that which has been accomplished by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the past, future, and present; even so it is for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions.
The Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra, one fascicle.
